statement: A long strip of paper has parallel straight edges. It is folded flat along a straight crease that makes an angle of 65° with the bottom edge. What acute angle do the edges of the folded-over part make with the edges of the part that stayed in place?

choices.misconception: I gave 90° - 65°, the angle between the crease and a line at right angles to the edge.
I thought the folded edge makes the same angle with the bottom edge as the crease does.
I gave 180° - 65°, the angle on the other side of the crease, without reflecting anything.
I found the angle $2 \times 65^\circ$ correctly but gave the obtuse angle instead of the acute one.

hints: Folding is a reflection in the crease.
A reflection keeps the angle with the mirror line the same size but puts it on the other side. Find the angle between the bottom edge and its reflection in the crease, then take the acute one.
The bottom edge makes 65° with the crease on one side, and its image makes 65° with the crease on the other side.

solutions.reliable: Folding reflects the folded part in the crease. The bottom edge makes $65^\circ$ with the crease, so its image makes $65^\circ$ with the crease on the other side. The angle between the edge and its image is $65^\circ + 65^\circ = 130^\circ$, so the acute angle between the two lines is $180^\circ - 130^\circ = 50^\circ$. The other edge of the folded part is parallel to this image, so it makes the same angle. The transferable idea: a fold is a reflection, and a reflection doubles the angle to the mirror line.

whyOnTest: A fold is a reflection, so the angle to the crease doubles, and the slips are forgetting to double it or giving the obtuse angle.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
